1.title: Single-Slit Diffraction
1.text:
Single-Slit Diffraction

A diffraction pattern is the pattern of bands made by interference of Huygens' wavelets passing through an opening.

Our big question for this lesson: how does a DVD make a rainbow? Let's start with a single slit. You already know light diffracts when it passes an edge. Huygens' principle explains why: every wavefront is made of many tiny point-source wavelets. Send light through a slit, which has two edges close together, and the wavelets interfere constructively and destructively, making a diffraction pattern on a screen.

When coherent green light passes through a single opening about 10 to 100 wavelengths wide, both edges diffract it, and bright and dark bands appear on a distant screen, as in Figure 12.

But this isn't Young's evenly spaced double-slit pattern. A single slit makes one wide, bright central band, with dimmer, narrower bands on either side. Switch to red light, and the central band gets wider, because red has a longer wavelength. With white light, the patterns for every color overlap: the center is white, with colored edges.

3.title: Huygens' Wavelets in a Slit
3.text:
Huygens' Wavelets in a Slit

Wavelets from paired points half a slit-width apart cancel to make dark bands.

To see how wavelets make the pattern, imagine a slit of width w split into an even number of Huygens' points, as in Figure 13. Each point is a source of wavelets. Now divide the slit into two equal halves, and pair one point from the top half with one from the bottom half, so the pair is w over 2 apart. Each pair makes coherent, cylindrical waves that interfere.

For every wavelet from the top half, there's a partner in the bottom half, w over 2 away, that can cancel it at a certain spot on the screen. When all such pairs cancel at the same spot, you get a dark band. So dark bands come from destructive interference of Huygens' wavelets.

Bright bands are where the pairs interfere constructively. And in the dim regions between bright and dark, there's partial destructive interference.

4.title: The Single-Slit Pattern
4.text:
The Single-Slit Pattern

The width of the central bright band is 2 x sub 1 equals 2 lambda L divided by w.

Light the slit, and a central bright band appears at point P sub zero, as in Figure 14. The first dark band is at P sub one. There, the path lengths r sub 1 and r sub 2 from a pair of wavelets differ by lambda over 2, half a wavelength, so they cancel.

The math is a lot like the double slit. With the screen much farther away than the slit width, and the two interfering sources w over 2 apart with a half-wavelength path difference, we get x sub 1 over L equals lambda over w. Here x sub 1 is the distance from the center of the bright band to the first dark band.

It's easier to measure the whole central band, which is 2 x sub 1 wide. So the width of the central bright band, 2 x sub 1, equals 2 times lambda times L, divided by w. Fun fact: if you compare single-slit and double-slit patterns using slits of the same width, the double-slit fringes fit inside the single-slit pattern. Double-slit patterns are really the interference of light from two single slits.

5.title: When Diffraction Shows Up
5.text:
When Diffraction Shows Up

Diffraction is noticeable when an opening is about 10 to 100 wavelengths wide.

The single-slit equation assumes the screen is much farther away than the slit is wide; in other words, L is much larger than w. That's what lets us use the small-angle simplifications.

Single-slit patterns show light's wave nature clearly when the slit is 10 to 100 times the wavelength. Bigger openings cast sharp shadows, as Isaac Newton first noticed.

The single-slit pattern does depend on wavelength, but its blurry bands make it a poor tool for measuring wavelength. For that, we put a whole lot of slits together.

6.title: Diffraction Gratings
6.text:
Diffraction Gratings

A diffraction grating is a device made of many small slits whose overlapping patterns form narrow, bright bands.

Diffraction gratings, like the one in Figure 15, are used for precise wavelength measurements. A diffraction grating is a device made of many small slits that diffract light and form a pattern of overlapping single-slit patterns. It looks like a double-slit pattern, but with much narrower, brighter bands. A grating can have as many as 10,000 slits per centimeter, so its slits can be just ten to the negative sixth meters apart.

One kind is a transmission grating, made by scratching very fine lines with a diamond point on glass that light passes through. The spaces between the scratches act as slits. Gratings are even etched into some diamonds to boost their dispersion and make them sparkle more.

Holographic gratings give the brightest spectra. A laser and mirrors make a pattern of parallel bright and dark lines on metal coated with light-sensitive material, which hardens where the light hits. Acid then eats away the unprotected metal, leaving hills and valleys matching the pattern. The metal can be used as a reflection grating, or pressed into heated plastic film. The smooth, wavy shape of the hills and valleys makes the patterns very bright.

7.title: Reflection Gratings and Optical Discs
7.text:
Reflection Gratings and Optical Discs

A reflection grating is a grating made by inscribing fine lines on a metallic or reflective surface.

You've probably seen rainbows shimmer off CDs, DVDs, or Blu-ray Discs, like in Figure 16. A grating made by inscribing fine lines on a metallic or reflective glass surface is a reflection grating, and optical discs are examples. Shine one color of light on a disc, and the reflected light makes a pattern on a screen. Transmission and reflection gratings make similar patterns and can be analyzed the same way.

A disc's surface is covered with lines of microscopic dents called pits, separated by flat areas called lands, arranged in a spiral. The closely spaced turns of that spiral act as a diffraction grating. And here's the answer to our focus question: when white light reflects off the spiral, each color interferes constructively at a different angle, so the colors fan out into a rainbow.

8.title: Storing and Reading Information
8.text:
Storing and Reading Information

Shorter laser wavelengths make smaller spots, so pits can be packed closer and discs hold more data.

A laser reads the pattern of pits and lands, a bit like a person reading braille with their fingertips. Light reflects from the disc into a detector. The laser is focused so a land reflects a bright spot onto the detector, while a pit spreads the light out, so the spot is dimmer.

Diffraction limits how small the laser spot can be. A shorter wavelength makes a smaller spot, so the pits can sit closer together and the disc holds more information. Music CDs use infrared light with a wavelength of 780 nanometers and hold about 700 megabytes. DVDs use red lasers at 650 nanometers and hold more than 4 gigabytes. Blu-ray Discs use violet lasers at 405 nanometers, which look blue and give the disc its name, and a single-layer disc holds up to 25 gigabytes.

So the shorter the wavelength used to read a disc, the more information it can store.

9.title: Measuring Wavelength with a Grating
9.text:
Measuring Wavelength with a Grating

For a grating, bright lines occur at m lambda equals d times the sine of theta.

A grating spectroscope, like Figure 17, measures wavelengths with a diffraction grating. Light from the source passes through a slit and a collimator, then the grating, and you view the pattern through a telescope.

With one color of light, a grating makes narrow, evenly spaced bright lines, as in Figure 18. The more slits per unit length, the narrower the lines, and the more precisely you can measure them. The grating pattern also has more dark space than the double-slit pattern, because there's more destructive interference, which narrows the lines even more.

We find the grating equation just like the double-slit one, with one difference: with a grating, theta can be large, so the small-angle simplification doesn't apply. Bright lines appear at angles where m times lambda equals d times the sine of theta, with m equal to 0, 1, 2, and so on, where d is the slit spacing. The central line is m equals 0. For the first-order line, the wavelength equals d times the sine of theta. Spectroscopists often use the m equals 2 or 3 lines, because they can measure the spacing between those more precisely.

10.title: Gratings and Gemstones
10.text:
Gratings and Gemstones

Gemologists use grating spectroscopes to identify stones by their pattern of bands.

Gemologists build diffraction gratings into spectroscopes to check gemstones. Experienced gemologists recognize the band patterns that white light makes after passing through different stones.

For example, three dark absorption bands, in the green, yellow, and orange parts of the spectrum, strongly suggest cobalt. That likely means a blue stone isn't a valuable sapphire or topaz at all, but a cheap piece of glass tinted blue with cobalt.

11.title: Example Problem 3, Using a DVD as a Diffraction Grating
11.text:
Example Problem 3, Using a DVD as a Diffraction Grating

Find theta from the tangent of theta equals x over L, then d equals lambda divided by the sine of theta.

A student notices the spectrum on a DVD. She aims her teacher's green laser pointer, with a wavelength of 532 nanometers, at the DVD and sees three bright spots on the wall. The spots are 1.29 meters apart, and the wall is 1.25 meters away. What's the spacing between the rows on the DVD?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch the DVD as a grating with the spots on the wall, and label the knowns. Known: x is 1.29 meters, L is 1.25 meters, and lambda is 532 nanometers. Unknown: d.

Step two: solve. Find the angle between the central spot and the next one using the tangent of theta equals x over L. Theta is the inverse tangent of 1.29 meters over 1.25 meters, which is 45.9 degrees. That's a big angle, so we can't use the small-angle shortcut. Now use lambda equals d times the sine of theta, so d equals lambda divided by the sine of theta. That's 532 times ten to the negative ninth meters, divided by the sine of 45.9 degrees, which is 7.41 times ten to the negative seventh meters, or 741 nanometers.

Step three: evaluate. The answer is in meters, right for a spacing. And since x and L are almost the same size, the angle is near 45 degrees, so d should be close to lambda, and it is.

testIt.how: Change the spot spacing on the wall (L = 1.25 m, λ = 532 nm).

12.title: Resolving Power of Lenses
12.text:
Resolving Power of Lenses

A circular aperture makes a central bright spot with rings: x sub 1 equals 1.22 lambda L divided by D.

The round lens of a telescope, a microscope, or even your eye is an opening, called an aperture, that light passes through. An aperture diffracts light just like a slit, but it makes a bright central spot surrounded by alternating bright and dark rings, as in Figure 19.

The equation is like the single-slit one. But a circle has one round edge instead of two straight ones, so the slit width w is replaced by the aperture diameter D, and a geometric factor of 1.22 appears. The distance to the first dark ring is x sub 1 equals 1.22 times lambda times L, divided by D.

testIt.how: Resize the circular aperture (λ = 550 nm, L = 1.0 m).

13.title: The Rayleigh Criterion
13.text:
The Rayleigh Criterion

Two sources are just resolved when the center of one image falls on the first dark ring of the other: x sub obj equals 1.22 lambda L sub obj divided by D.

When a telescope looks at a distant star, diffraction spreads the star's image into a little blob. Two stars close together can blur into one. In 1879, Lord Rayleigh, a British physicist, mathematician, and later Nobel Prize winner, set a rule for telling one star from two.

The Rayleigh criterion says that if the center of one source's bright spot falls on the first dark ring of the other, the two images are at the limit of resolution. At that limit, a viewer can just tell there are two stars instead of one.

How far apart are two such objects? In Figure 20, similar triangles give x sub obj over L sub obj equals x sub 1 over L. Combine that with x sub 1 over L equals 1.22 lambda over D, and the separation between objects at the limit of resolution is x sub obj equals 1.22 times lambda times L sub obj, divided by D. Here L sub obj is the distance from the aperture to the objects.

14.title: Diffraction in the Eye
14.text:
Diffraction in the Eye

The eye's resolution limit is set by its pupil diameter and the spacing of cones in the retina.

In bright light, your pupil is about 3 millimeters across, and your eye is most sensitive to yellow-green light, around 550 nanometers. Plug those into the Rayleigh criterion, and x sub obj is about 2 times ten to the negative fourth times L sub obj.

The pupil is about 2 centimeters from the retina. Using x sub 1 equals 1.22 lambda L over D, two barely resolved points make bright spots about 4 micrometers apart on the retina. The cones, the retina's light detectors, are about 2 micrometers apart in the fovea, the sharpest part of the retina. So ideally, three cones in a row record light, dark, and light, as in Figure 21. The eye seems built just right!

By this rule, your eye could separate two car headlights 1.5 meters apart from 7 kilometers away. In practice, though, imperfections in the lens and the fluid inside the eye make the smallest separation you can actually resolve about five times larger than the Rayleigh limit. The brain's vision centers limit how well we spot tiny points too.

testIt.how: Drive two headlights 1.5 m apart away from you.

15.title: Scientific Breakthroughs, Beckoning Bees with Blue Halos
15.text:
Scientific Breakthroughs, Beckoning Bees with Blue Halos

Disordered nanoscale ridges on some petals diffract light into a blue halo that bees can see.

Studies show that several kinds of bees prefer flowers in the blue part of the spectrum, which their eyes are tuned to see. Many plants can't make blue pigment, but some have a clever trick: tiny ridges on their petals bend and scatter light to make a blue halo, like the flower in the photo.

Scientists studied these nanostructures with microscopes, including scanning electron microscopes, and computer models showed the ridges vary in height and spacing. That disorder, as physicists call it, diffracts light into iridescent blue and ultraviolet wavelengths. The more variation, the stronger the halo. Many unrelated flower species evolved these structures on their own, an example of natural selection causing convergent evolution.

To test the idea, scientists built artificial flowers with copies of the nanostructures. Bees could tell otherwise identical flowers apart by the blue halo alone, and found the haloed flowers faster. Faster foraging means more pollination, which is a big survival advantage. Try drawing the ridges on a petal and explaining, in your own words, how they diffract light.
